In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Hujurat (The Private Chambers)

Its purpose is guidance to noble character by honouring the Prophet ﷺ through good manners towards him in himself and in his community, and by preserving that reverence outwardly, so that it serves as a sign of what is inward, and is thereby called faith (îmân). Likewise, faith in Allah requires the performance of outward acts and submission to them with their conditions, pillars and limits, so that they may be a clear evidence of what is inward and a witness-proof for it. ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 1] ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 2]. The essential purpose of the surah, then, is to watch over one's conduct towards the Prophet ﷺ, because it is the first of the mufassal (the later, shorter surahs), which is a summary of the Qur'an, just as the purpose of al-Fatihah, which is the first of the Qur'an, is watchfulness over Allah. The second surah of the mufassal begins with one of the disjointed letters (al-muqatta'at), just as the second of the rest of the surahs begins with disjointed letters. Its name, al-Hujurat, clearly indicates this by what its verse "bismillah" indicates: Allah, the King, the Compeller, the Majestic, who is not pleased with any deed from one who neglects the exaltation of His Messenger ﷺ; "al-Rahman" (the Most Gracious), whose general mercy includes establishing good manners as a means of reaching a good return; "al-Rahim" (the Most Merciful), who has singled out people of understanding to turn towards what brings them a fine reward.

* *

When He, glorified be He, honoured the Prophet ﷺ in the surah of Qital (Muhammad) by mentioning him at its beginning by his noble name, named the surah after him, filled the surah of Muhammad with his exaltation, concluded it with his name, and praised his followers on his account, He opened this surah with the requirement of good manners towards him in word and deed, so that one may be counted among his party and attain nearness to him. The basis of this is the lofty qualities of character, which are either towards Allah, glorified and exalted be He, or towards His Messenger ﷺ, or towards others, though each category does not fail to touch on the others. The others are either within the ranks of obedience to the believers or outside it, and that is the wrongdoer (fasiq). The one who enters into the obedience of the believers and follows their way is either present with them or absent from them. These make five categories, and the address (nida') was divided by these into five occurrences, each one for a category of them. He opened with Allah, because good manners towards Him are the comprehensive principle for all of them and the foundation upon which nothing else can be built. He said, addressing those marked by the first of the teeth of the heart (i.e., the first stage of faith), to indicate that the cause of the revelation of these verses lay in their own actions and not in the actions of the people of perfection; so it is a slip that is spoken of, and it is what ought not to have been said. So that the address, which is customary for the lowest of them, even with hypocrisy, would include those above them a fortiori: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, meaning, those who professed faith, ﴿do not put forward﴾. He omitted the object so that it would cover everything that may correctly be put forward, so that the mind goes in every direction. It is also possible that the omission is intended in itself, and that the prohibition is directed at the act of putting forward itself; that is, do not engage in this action. It is also possible that it comes from qaddama, with the doubled letter, in the sense of aqdama and taqaddama, that is, to encourage oneself to advance; and from it comes muqaddimat al-jaysh (the vanguard of the army), and they are its forward ones. He also pointed out the reprehensibility of what they were forbidden and the depiction of its enormity, and that they are in His grasp, as a warning to them, so He said: ﴿before Allah﴾, meaning the King whose vengeance cannot be borne.

Since the context concerns the prohibition of putting forward and advancing, and the requirement of the message is to execute the commands and prohibitions from the King without the one addressed making any objection at all, and for this reason it is necessary that nothing important be spoken in His presence and nothing important be done except with His permission, because servants, owing to their deficiency, have no independence in anything at all, He expressed it with "Messenger" rather than "Prophet" after mentioning His greatest name, as an increase in depicting the exaltation, and said: ﴿and His Messenger﴾, meaning, the one whose greatness is very manifest. For this reason He joined his name with His name and his mention with His mention. This is a preparation for what follows of his exaltation. Thus the expression by this is an indication that the soul, when left to its original nature, is filled, merely by seeing him, with awe of him and reverence for him, so no one does otherwise except by encouraging himself to do so and forcing it against what the upright original nature calls for. The meaning, then, is: do not be those who advance in anything at all, and Allah speaks the truth and guides to the way, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conveys from Him and does not speak from desire. So for others, following and imitation are required, not initiating and innovating, whether the Prophet ﷺ is absent or present, by death or otherwise.

For indeed his traces are like his eye. Whoever exerts effort in them is guided to what is most righteous,

﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 69].

And when He borrowed the expression of "two hands" to indicate power, and depicted the clear evidence as a warning against the vengeance of the Able when He is opposed, He stated this explicitly with His saying, exalted be He: ﴿and fear Allah﴾, meaning, place between yourselves and the wrath of the Greatest King a shield, for taqwa (God-consciousness) prevents you from neglecting His right, opposing His command, and advancing upon something whose pleasure you do not know concerning it.

Since He, glorified be He, is with each one by His knowledge, and nearer to him than his own self, yet He is pure unseen, because He is veiled by the cloak of pride and the garment of majesty and dominance, and since a human being forgets what is out of his sight, He mentioned it, warning with His saying, beginning anew or giving a reason, emphasizing, to draw attention to what is in that of strangeness and greatness, which it is right for a human being to strive against his own self for the sake of, in belief in Him and persistence in continually keeping Him in mind, because the acts of the disobedient are the acts of one who denies Him: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, meaning, the One who has comprehensive attributes of perfection. And since what precedes it is either speech or action, He said: ﴿is All-Hearing﴾, meaning, of your words, whether you say them, ﴿All-Knowing﴾, meaning, of your deeds before you do them.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When He, glorified be He, described His chosen servants, the companions of His Prophet and those specially distinguished by the virtue of seeing him and the noble company with him, saying: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves﴾ [Al-Fath: 29] "to the end of it," He praised them and mentioned His description of them with this in the Torah and the Gospel. This is a distinction which they alone possessed with the honour of its nobility, and it followed the clear meaning of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110], to the end of it. It testified to them of their great station with Him. This was suitable for a demand that they fulfil the branches of faith in word and deed, outwardly and inwardly, with the clearest action and the most sincere intention, and that they be purified from what came from them in addressing their prophets, such as the saying of the Children of Israel: ﴿O Moses, invoke your Lord for us﴾ [Al-A'raf: 134], and [to] what witnessed of this kind their bad condition. So He, exalted be He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾, the verse. And ﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak loudly to him in speech﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 2], to His saying: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 5]. So they were asked for manners befitting the loftiness of their faith, even if some of it might be forgiven to others who are not at their level. It has been said: "The good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near." So it is as if it was said to them: Do not neglect what has been granted to you in the Torah and the Gospel, for it is a station which no other nation has attained, so respond to it by purifying your actions from any suspicion that their apparent forms arose from carelessness in address or ill intent in reply. Make your outward and inward match, and let your public conduct reveal the soundness of your hidden hearts. ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah—those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 3]. Then they were made aware of the bad condition of one who deviated from this quality, so He, exalted be He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who call you from behind the private chambers—most of them do not reason﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 4]. Then they were commanded to verify at the moment of Satan's incitement or of a slanderous lie: ﴿O you who have believed, if a wrongdoer brings you news, investigate﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 6], the verse. Then He commanded them to set right their mutual relations and to cooperate in that by fighting the rebellious transgressors, to improve companionship, and to adopt what yields love, affection of faith, and humility, and that all good lies in taqwa: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [Al-Hujurat: 13]. All of this is a warning against the loss of the lofty qualities for which they were described at the end of Surat al-Fath.

And when the honouring of the Messenger (ﷺ) was established, by forbidding that anyone act on his behalf in matters that are his own responsibility, such as taking the lead in affairs and settling important matters, so that he is addressed only in answer or by question concerning a necessary matter that cannot be postponed, and since whoever speaks to him for such a purpose may raise his voice more than is fitting for anyone else of lesser station, and since among his circumstances was that revelation came to him concerning great matters, and raising the voice at that time would disturb the good reception of revelation, along with the lack of respect and the omission of reverence and honouring it entails, He said, mentioning the second of the divisions, which is that in which the primary consideration is his station (ﷺ), (p-356) deducing from what preceded of his description with prophethood, which indicates prophecy, commanding the preservation of his sanctity and the observance of courtesy in serving and accompanying him, by exalting, magnifying, strengthening and honouring him. He repeats the call to them with what they bound themselves to, namely obedience to him through affirming him, and as a call to renewed help and a reminder of the urgency of attentive listening, and as an indication that the one being addressed has a matter that deserves to be singled out for the address and to be given separate instruction: ﴿O you who believe﴾, repeating the designation by the lowest of the ranks of hearts, to alert that the one who commits such prohibited acts, and who needs to be warned by the prohibition, has already done so, one whose state is this. ﴿Do not raise your voices﴾, that is, in anything whatsoever, ﴿above the voice of the Prophet﴾, that is, the one who receives from Allah, and his receiving from Him is expected at every time. This indicates that harming the scholars whom Allah has prepared to receive the understanding of His religion from him is very grave, for disturbing their times prevents them from much of that.

When he had explained what is due in this regard because of prophethood, he explained what is due in his own person of excellence, and said: ﴿And do not speak loudly to him in speech﴾, that is, when you address him, whether in a voice like his or lower than his voice, for that is not suitable to what great people are held in awe by and what the eminent are venerated with. When this included every particular kind of loud speech, namely that which removes excellence, He said: ﴿as you speak loudly to one another﴾, that is, if you do not do that, no difference will appear between the Prophet (ﷺ) and anyone else. When He forbade that, He explained its harm, saying, clarifying that among deeds there are those that nullify and it is not known that they nullify, so that the doer is like one walking on a dangerous path who [still] keeps guarding against its danger and maintains his caution: ﴿lest﴾, that is, the prohibition is for the sake of [fear] that ﴿your deeds be nullified﴾, that is, be corrupted and thus fall, ﴿those [which are] the deeds in reality, which are all the good deeds﴾, ﴿while you are unaware﴾, that is, that they have been nullified. For when a person becomes bold in this, he treats it lightly, and when he treats it lightly he persists in it, and when he persists in it he is close to treating the one addressed lightly, and so he disbelieves while he is unaware.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 49, verse 3:

When He, glorified be He, had preceded (the prohibition) against violating anything of the sanctity due to him (ﷺ), and had forbidden raising the voice and speaking loudly in the manner described, He produced reverence in his presence as a form of veneration. He then explained what awaits those who observe this great courtesy. He said, emphasizing (the matter) because among the hypocrites and others there are those who deny it, and as an alert that, because of God's love for him and His pleasure with him, he is worthy that his command be emphasized and that its performance be kept constant: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices﴾, i.e., they soften and subdue them, out of the tranquility that has settled upon them from awe of his presence. Al-Tabari (al-Tabari) said: the origin of ghadd is restraint with gentleness, ﴿their voices﴾ in humility, submission (p-358), observance of courtesy, and reverence.

Since the one conveying a message may be distracted by noise and raised voices from what he intended to convey, (the Prophet (ﷺ) said): "Indeed, the Night of Power was shown to me, and I came out to inform you of it, but two men were quarrelling, so it was made to slip from my mind, and perhaps it is better for you." He said: ﴿in the presence of the Messenger of God﴾, i.e., the one whose speech by nature rises above every (other) speech, because he is a conveyer from the Supreme King. He used the expression "in the presence of" (ʿinda), which is for the apparent (rank), to indicate that the people of this special presence do not produce anything except the most perfect courtesy.

When He began mentioning them with emphasis, as an alert to the greatness of what they were called to, He increased this in magnitude by pointing to them with the distal demonstrative, saying: ﴿Those﴾, i.e., those of elevated rank, because of their lofty aspirations in submitting to the one whom their Lord has sent, the One from whom alone they recognize any goodness: ﴿those whom God has tested﴾, i.e., the act of the One encompassing all attributes of perfection, (acting as) one who tests through intense association with hardships, in a manner that leads to a gift of gentleness, purity from every stain, expansion and breadth, ﴿their hearts﴾, so He purified them ﴿for taqwa﴾, i.e., fear that leads its bearer to prepare by establishing what protects him from every disliked thing. Imtihan (testing) is an intensive examination that leads to knowledge of the outcome. The meaning is that He purified their hearts and cleansed them (p-359), as the goldsmith tests gold and silver by melting them for purification and removing every adulteration, in order to bring out what is hidden within them of taqwa, so that it becomes known to creation in the world of witnessing, as it was already known to Him, glorified be He, in the world of the unseen. This is their departure from ordinary human habits and their separation from what natural disposition requires, and it is the reality of monotheism (tawhid). Taqwa does not appear except at times of trials and hardships, through obligations and other things, and it is not established except by constant obedience in ease and in hardship, and by departing from such (ordinary inclinations).

Since a human being, however much he strives in goodness, is still a place of deficiency, He resumed the report of their reward with His words, dropping the particle of causation (fa') from it, indicating that this is purely by His generosity: ﴿For them there is forgiveness﴾, i.e., for their lapses and slips, ﴿and a great reward﴾, i.e., a recompense that cannot be described, for the excellence of what they did.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 49, verse 4:

When He, glorified is He, had forbidden violating good manners, and commanded preserving reverence, and mentioned the description of the obedient, He followed that, by way of consequence, with the description of the one who violated it. He said, emphasizing (because their condition was that of one who lacks complete intellect): ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you﴾, meaning: they renew their calling to you without repentance, while the situation is that their calling to you occurs ﴿from behind﴾. The affirmation of this preposition indicates that he (ﷺ) was inside them; had it been dropped, that would not have conveyed this, but would have conveyed (p-360) that the relation of the places behind which the chambers lie is equal, with respect to him and to them, and that is by all of them being outside them. And "behind" (al-waraa') is the direction which conceals you and conceals them, from behind or in front.

Since the Messenger (ﷺ) was, in himself and in conveying the messages of Allah in their form, at a level of greatness such that it is not hidden from anyone, no one has the right to presume over him in them, nor to hasten him away from anything. His calling from behind one chamber was, for this reason, like his calling from behind every chamber. He said in the plural: ﴿the chambers﴾, and did not attach them to him out of reverence for him, and so that it would include my existence in other than them too. The meaning: beginning the calling from a direction in which the chambers lie between you and them, so that they are facing you from them and you from them. "Hujurat" is the plural of "hujrah" (chamber), which is a piece of land enclosed by a wall that prevents harm, by word or deed, from whoever is outside it toward whoever is inside it; for it is in what is particular to him, such as being alone with his wives or attending to some matter of his condition, which cannot be arranged with people present, in what the manliness requires. He attributed the verb to the plural, though the caller was only some of them, because of their contentment with it or their silence regarding the prohibition.

Since the one who is silent [may not be content], he said: ﴿most of them﴾, meaning (p-361) the caller and the content, [to the exclusion of] the silent one, for an excuse, ﴿do not reason﴾, because they did not show patience, but rather acted toward him (ﷺ) as some of them act toward one who is their equal, and intellect prevents such a thing toward one who is characterized by leadership. How much more so when the leadership is that of prophethood and messengership from the King, the One, the Subduer.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 49, verse 5:

When He censured them for the evil of their conduct, He guided them to that by which they would be praised for its goodness, saying: ﴿And if they had been patient﴾, that is, the callers and those who were content, ﴿until you came out﴾, that is, they restrained themselves and held themselves back from calling out to him. Patience (sabr) is the restraining of the self from being drawn after its desires, and it is a restraint that involves hardship. And "sabr 'an kadha" (patience concerning such-and-such) has its verb omitted due to its frequent occurrence, meaning "patience of himself" (nafsahu). ﴿until you came out﴾ to them of your own accord, when you have finished with what concerns you of the matters that come to you from the Truth and the welfare of creation. Since going out might be for other beneficial purposes, and it is not proper in good manners to cut that off for him, He said: ﴿to them﴾, meaning: it is not for them to speak to you until you are free for them and turn toward them, for you do nothing out of its proper time, in accordance with the requirement of the mission. ﴿it would have been﴾, that is, the patience, ﴿better for them﴾.

Since the Arabs were people of high aspiration, they are such that they accept only the best, so He said: ﴿better for them﴾, that is, than their hastening to wake you at the time of midday heat, and than what would have happened had they knocked on the door with their fingernails as other companions, may Allah be pleased with them, used to do. (p-362) This is on the assumption that what they supposed to be good in it was indeed good, and that they were understanding. So in expressing it this way, together with fairness, indeed overlooking and kindness, there is a stirring of them toward high aspirations and a guidance to that for which they would boast of good qualities. Al-Razi said: Abu 'Uthman said: good manners in the presence of the great carry their possessor to the lofty ranks and to good in this world and the Hereafter. End of quote. The excellence of patience in religion is well known. As for in this world, if they had shown good manners toward their Lord, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have increased them in bounty, so he freed all their captives and increased them. The verse is of the type of ihtibak (interlocking omission): he omitted the reason for the lack of patience at first because of what was indicated by it second, and the intellect second, because of what was indicated by its mention first.

When He mentioned the supposition as a discipline for us and a training in pardoning the ignorant and excusing and teaching him, He said: ﴿But they did not have patience and they behaved badly, and that was worse for them; and Allah is All-Knowing of what they do, Most Forbearing﴾, in that He did not hasten to punish them for their bad manners toward His Messenger (ﷺ). He joined to it, seeking their goodwill while implying a warning: ﴿And Allah is﴾, that is, the One encompassing the attributes of perfection, ﴿Oft-Forgiving﴾, that is, Concealing of the sin of whoever repents from his ignorance, ﴿Most Merciful﴾, who deals with him in the manner of the merciful, bestowing upon him His blessings. When they repented, Allah reconciled them regarding their harshness toward the best of His creation by making them the most severe of people against the worst of people: the Dajjal; for the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed they (p-363) are the most severe of people against him."

When Allah, glory be to Him, finished what He intended by the prohibition against harming the Messenger ﷺ personally, and this included harming his community, He said: "It grieves him that you suffer" [9:128]. Whoever harmed them was a *fasiq* (a deviant transgressor). The greatest harm to them is what causes distress and stirs up war. People with ulterior motives might use these courtesies as a pretext to harm some of the Muslims. They would accuse them of neglecting some of them, and then they themselves would fall into what they had accused others of: neglecting the Messenger's right, and failing to adhere to his allegiance and servitude. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had such pure character and such manifest nobility that one could be sure he would not place anything in other than its proper place, or command something that was not lawful. This is in addition to his *ʿiṣmah* (infallibility, divine protection from error). Here, drawing attention to what is in the third category of noble character, namely refraining from weakness by relying on the reports of deviants, He spoke. It addresses everyone who has affirmed faith, by way of inference from what has preceded. It urges seeking guidance through reason, the faculty He denied to the people of the previous verse, along with pardoning the wrongdoer and showing mercy to the servants of Allah. He called them with the particle of distance, indicating that whoever needs to be explicitly told such a warning, and is not content with what he has gained from the principles of the Sharia, has placed himself in a distant position. It also alerts that what falls within this scope is a matter of great gravity and a weighty consequence: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. He used the past tense, which is for the lowest degree of hearts [of belief]. He used the particle of doubt, signaling that deviants among them are few and that they rarely come to them with a report that carries weight. So He said: ﴿If there comes to you﴾, that is, at any time, ﴿a deviant﴾, that is, one who has gone out of the bond of religion, whatever deviant he may be, ﴿with a report﴾, that is, news whose matter is grave, so that it produces evil, whatever good it may contain, if it is of this kind. ﴿Then verify﴾, that is, apply yourselves to clarification, which is distinguishing error from correctness, by using the natural faculty of reason which was denied to those being addressed, and by being characterized by forgiveness and mercy, ﴿so that Allah may have mercy upon you and forgive you﴾. This recitation is the goal of the recitation of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, which uses the *thāʾ* with three dots, then the *yāʾ* with two dots above (i.e., *fatabayyanū* read as *fatathabbatū*, "then be firm and careful"). The context guides that the report of a deviant, like a slanderer or one who spreads corruption, is not accepted, and therefore it is not rejected outright until it is tested. It also guides that the report of a trustworthy person needs no hesitation, otherwise he would be equal to the deviant. Thus, the caution is caused by deviance. When that is absent, and no other cause that requires caution exists, acceptance is obligatory. Something made conditional on a word such as *in* ("if") is absent when its condition is absent. Clarification takes one of two forms: by consulting the Prophet ﷺ if he is present, or by consulting his traces in the Book of Allah and His Sunnah, until the matter becomes clear from these two, [if he is absent], for indeed no event ever occurs except that the Book and the Sunnah contain a way out of it.

When He commanded clarification, He mentioned its reason, saying: ﴿lest you harm﴾, that is, out of dislike that you should harm ﴿a people﴾, that is, people who, with their beneficial strength for the people of Islam, are innocent of what is attributed to them, ﴿in ignorance﴾, that is, while being ignorant of the state that would merit such treatment.

Since a person who places something in other than its proper place is deserving of regret, He made the following statement a consequence of that: ﴿then you become﴾, that is, then you become, but He expressed it this way because the most dreadful regret is that which confronts a person in the morning, at the time of his alertness, leisure, and turning toward his pleasures: ﴿regretful for what you have done﴾, that is, for having harmed them, ﴿regretful﴾, that is, deeply immersed in grief over what has passed, from what Allah causes in your souls of matters that make hearts tremble and natures weaken. That is His practice regarding every falsehood, for since it is unstable in itself, nothing arises from it except instability and regret over what has happened, along with wishing it had not happened. This is a distress that accompanies a person as a companion with a lasting duration, from what its root ("madana" and "damina") indicates. It arises from squandering the weighty means that a person has been commanded to strive for, as the hadith (a saying of the Prophet ﷺ) indicates: "Be keen on what benefits you, and do not be incapable. If something overcomes you, say: 'Allah has decreed, and He does what He wills,' and do not say: 'If only I had done such and such,' for 'if only' opens the work of Satan." The deviant mentioned in the verse is intended as a category, and the one by whose cause this verse was revealed was al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah. He continued in this manner until 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, appointed him over Kufa. He led the people in the dawn prayer while intoxicated, performing four rak'ahs, then said: "[Shall I add more?]" [p. 366] So 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, dismissed him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 49, verse 7:

Since their rushing ahead in many matters without consulting the one whom God sent as a mercy to His servants, so that He might inform them of what they should do and what they should leave undone, was the action of one who does not know that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is near to him, and since turning away from him while he was alive, and from exerting effort to derive matters from his Shari'ah after his death, was a corrupting matter for the bond (between them) if it were not taken as a lesson and given the utmost attention, He informed them of it, placing them in the position of one who does not know that he (the Prophet) is present with him, and by using the word of alerting (kalimat al-tanbih) He indicated that whoever neglects observing this is counted among the heedless. So He said: ﴿And know﴾, that is, O community. He placed the information first, as a notification that some of them, through their objecting or through their rushing ahead into what they have no knowledge of, act as one who does not know the measure of what God has singled them out with, of His bounty to them through him (ﷺ). Thus it conveys a rebuke of whoever did that: ﴿that among you﴾, [that is], in the sense of specific address to you, and how great an honour that is.

﴿the Messenger of God﴾, that is, the Greatest King, characterized by majesty and honour, in a state in which you want him to follow your wishes. This is a very shameful matter, for it is not fitting that he should move except by the command of the One who sent him. So it is obligatory upon you to return from that state, for you are more ignorant than you are knowledgeable. And because of their desire that he should not obey them in all matters, He expressed it in the present tense, saying: ﴿If he were to obey you﴾, while he does not love your distress or anything that would burden you, ﴿in many matters﴾ (p-367), that is, those which you want him to do, namely that he should act in incidents according to what occurs to you and what you deem correct, so that his action with you would be the action of one who obeys another and follows him. Then the situation would be reversed, the one being followed would become a follower, and the one obeyed would become obedient. ﴿you would surely be distressed﴾, that is, you would be destroyed and perish. Whoever always wants the command of the Messenger (ﷺ) to be subordinate to his own command, Satan has made disbelief attractive to him, and those are the misguided. The context of "if" (law) definitively indicates that the implied sense is: but he (ﷺ) does not obey you, out of aversion to what would burden you, because of his character of obedience to God, of standing at His limits, and of restraining all his movements and stillnesses by His command, together with his insight in distinguishing between what confuses and his complete experience with ambiguous matters, which are the cause of the destruction of most people because many do not know them. The restriction to "many" indicates that they hit the right course in many matters.

Since the implied sense is necessarily, as the context guides: "And if you had opposed him in the matters in which he does not obey you, you would have been distressed," He (God) then made an exception to his saying: ﴿But God﴾, that is, the Greatest King who does what He wills, ﴿has made faith beloved to you﴾, so you adhered to his obedience and fell in love with following him. And since a person may love something while knowing a defect in it, and thus be liable to waver concerning it, He negated that by His saying: (p-368) ﴿and has made it appealing in your hearts﴾, that is, so nothing is more beautiful in your view than it, nothing equals it, and nothing approaches it in any way. ﴿and has made disbelief hateful to you﴾, which is covering up the truth that the original nature and the minds free from desire lead to, by denial, ﴿and defiance﴾, which is slipping out of the bond of religion, even without covering up, but without reflection, ﴿and disobedience﴾, which is refusing to submit in general. Thus you did not oppose him, and you regarded opposing him as destruction, so you became, and to God belongs the favour, the most obedient of things to the Messenger (ﷺ). From this it is known that God, the Exalted, alone is the Doer of all actions, of acts of obedience and sins, of customs and acts of worship, because He is the Creator of each. They were praised for God's action in them because they are the apparent doers. So it stands in the place of: "You obeyed the Messenger (ﷺ) and did not oppose him." [And the act of God was placed] — though they are not praised for it — in the place of their own act for which they are praised, to urge gratitude and to free oneself from self-admiration.

Since the context guided to following them in this manner, it produced His saying, praising them a second time, shifting the speech from addressing them to addressing him (ﷺ), to show the greatness of these attributes, and He expressed it with the demonstrative of distance to indicate the high rank of the one characterized: ﴿Those﴾ [that is] those whose measures God, the Capable of everything, has raised. ﴿They are﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿the rightly guided﴾, that is, those who are perfect in right guidance, which is guidance in the best manner and measure. In the tafsir of al-Asfahani: "Rushd is steadfastness upon the path of truth (p-369) together with firmness in it." End of quote.

What produced rectitude is following the truth, for God has guaranteed for whoever deliberately seeks good and strives against his own soul in righteousness, hitting what is correct and perfecting his efforts, which is incompatible with regret.

﴿And those who strive in Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths. And indeed, God is with the doers of good﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 69]. The context has indicated that in the report about al-Walid they were two groups: one group believed him and wanted the expedition against Banu al-Mustaliq and advised it, and another group hesitated. And that both groups in the end submitted to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so they were guided. Thus the verse is of the type called ihtibak (a figure in which two contrasting parts are mutually implied, one being left unstated and understood from the other), and it resembles it: the conditional in ﴿If he were to obey you﴾ indicated the adversative, and the adversative in ﴿But God﴾ indicated the conditional clearly.

Having mentioned the endearing, the beautifying and the making hateful, and the guidance they produced, He mentioned their cause, to inform that He, exalted is He, is under no obligation to do anything, and to urge gratitude. So He said: ﴿Grace﴾, i.e., increase, bounty, and great, magnificent favor, and an elevated rank from Allah, the King, the Greatest, in whose hand is every thing; ﴿and blessing﴾, [i.e.,] a good, pleasant, comfortable life, ease, tranquility, and honor.

Since the sense is: Allah bestows blessings by His grace, in whose hand is every harm and benefit, He joined to it His saying: ﴿And Allah﴾, i.e., the One encompassing the attributes of perfection, ﴿is All-Knowing﴾, i.e., of all-encompassing knowledge, so He knows the states of the believers and the differences among them; ﴿All-Wise﴾, of perfect wisdom, so He places things in their most suitable and most precise places. Therefore He placed His blessing of the Messengership and faith according to His knowledge and wisdom. (p-370)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on Surah 49, verse 9:

Since tale-bearing (*namimah*) and the transmission of false and blameworthy reports often lead to strife (*fitan*) and bring about fighting, and since the All-Knowing, All-Wise does not establish a cause without mentioning its effect and pointing to its remedy, and does not forbid a thing except to one who is disposed to it because of the inclination toward it within his nature, so that he may at times actually commit it, God, Exalted is He, said, teaching us the method of wisdom in averting what false reports lead to of fighting, expressing it with the particle of doubt (*in*) to indicate that [what] falls within its scope should not occur among them, nor should they mention it except as a supposition: ﴿And if two groups﴾, that is, two groups in actuality or potentiality, each of which is worthy of gathering around what has befallen them from the ruler, such that, because of the intensity of their attachment to him, they become like the group surrounding him and gathered about him, so that from the intensity of their gathering upon that, one cannot tell the first of them from the last, ﴿of the believers﴾, that is, of those who are counted among the most steadfast in faith, whether he himself is steadfast or merely one who performs what is called by that name only.

Since the abomination and corruption are greater in fighting between groups, He expressed it with the plural pronoun rather than the dual, portraying it in the ugliest form, and so said: ﴿fight﴾, [that is] they become mixed up through fighting until they are like a single faction. ﴿Then make peace﴾, that is, (p-٣٧١) then bring about reconciliation so that peace may be achieved. Since what matters in reconciliation, when it takes place between the two groups, is that what calms the evil occurs, even if a few individuals from either side remain behind and are of no account, He expressed it with the dual rather than the plural, saying: ﴿between them﴾, that is, by admonition and guidance in both worldly and otherworldly matters. And do not suppose that the transgressor is not a believer, lest you overstep God's command concerning him.

Since transgression (*baghy*) is among the most reprehensible of matters, and it ought not to be attributed to anyone, He expressed it with the particle of doubt, guiding toward that, and so said: ﴿But if one of them transgresses﴾, that is, the evil intention arising from the souls that command evil ﴿transgresses﴾ causes one of them ﴿against the other﴾, that is, the two groups, ﴿so that it does not return to the judgment of God from which it departed and did not accept the truth. Since the pronoun here might perhaps create ambiguity, and a contentious person might seize upon it in the matter of corruption, He removed every ambiguity by explicit mention, and so said: ﴿then fight﴾, that is, bring about and seek the fighting of ﴿the one that﴾

Since fighting is not permissible except with continued transgression, He expressed it with the present tense, to make clear that whenever transgression ceases, even by repentance and without force, fighting becomes forbidden, and so said: ﴿that transgresses﴾, that is, it brings about the intention and persists in it; and continue fighting it ﴿until it returns﴾, that is, returns from what it has come to of the drawing of severance, which is like the heat of the sun, when the shade has displaced it, to what it was in of righteousness and goodness, which is like the shade that displaces the sun. This is the meaning of His saying, (p-٣٧٢) Exalted is He: ﴿to the command of God﴾, that is, [adhering to] what the King commanded, who does not neglect the wrongdoer, but must surely requite him, and His command is what was upon justice before the transgression. Since fighting the transgressor is deserving of returning him, He indicated this by His saying: ﴿And if it returns﴾, that is, returns to what it was upon of holding fast to the command of God, which is justice, ﴿then make peace﴾, that is, bring about reconciliation ﴿between them﴾.

Since dispute generally draws, in speech and deed, what produces resentment in the reconcilers toward some of the disputants, which would be taken as inclining toward one party against another, He said: ﴿with justice﴾, and let the fighting not lead you to rancor toward those who fight, lest you act unjustly. Since justice in such a matter is hard on souls because of the grudges they bear, God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and act justly﴾, that is, remove *qast* (with fatha, which means injustice) by doing *qist* (with kasra, which is great justice in which there is no injustice), in that matter and in all your affairs. Then He gave the reason, encouraging it, by His saying, emphasizing it as an alert that this is among the greatest of praiseworthy qualities, and as a refutation of one who might say that only the weak bind themselves to uphold it: ﴿Indeed, God﴾, that is, He in whose hand is victory and abandonment, ﴿loves those who act justly﴾, that is, He treats the people of justice with honor in the manner of one who loves.

When He commanded what may lead to fighting, and the aggressor may be closer to reconciliation by way of kinship than the one who was wronged, this was taken into account. Since fighting is a difficult matter that may deter people from reconciliation, He, glorified is He, gave the reason for this by placing the kinship of religion above the kinship of lineage. He fully disclosed that it is not permissible to abandon this reconciliation, because doing so leads to the scattering of unity, which leads to the weakening of Islam and its people, which leads to the manifestation of falsehood, which leads to the greatest corruption, for which there is no remedy. So He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the believers are but brothers﴾, meaning all of them, even if their lineages, aims and lands are far apart, ﴿brothers﴾ because they are affiliated with one origin, which is faith. There is no distance between them, and none of them is superior to another in any respect other than faith.

Since brotherhood necessarily calls to reconciliation, He made His saying ﴿so make reconciliation﴾ a consequence of it.

Since the term "ṭāʾifah" (group) may be applied to what is a foundation around which one circles, just as it is applied to what has the capacity for shaving and circumambulation, and since the least that this can be is two, and since their quarrel draws on a quarrel between two groups, in that each side is angered by people of its own tribe and companions, He said, placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun for emphasis in establishing and confirming the matter, and to inform that what is meant by "ṭāʾifah" is strength and not the act, so that it includes the two and whatever is above them: ﴿between your two brothers﴾, meaning those who differ, through fighting or otherwise, just as you reconcile between your two brothers by lineage. ﴿And if you do not do so, there will be fitnah (strife) on earth and great corruption.﴾ Indeed, the matter is as it has been reported from Abu ʿUthman al-Hiri, that the brotherhood of religion is more firmly established than the brotherhood of lineage. Yaʿqub read ﴿ikhwatikum﴾ with the plural, but the reading of the majority is more eloquent, because it indicates by direct implication the two and whatever is above them. ﴿And fear Allah﴾, meaning the Greatest King whose servants they are, in reconciling between them by fighting or otherwise; do not do what has the outward appearance of reconciliation while its inward reality is corruption. He pointed to the ease of matters with Him, the effectiveness of His command, and that souls aspire only to honour, not to its coming from a specific source. Therefore He framed His saying in the passive: ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾, meaning: so that when you do this, you may be in hope within yourselves and in the eyes of those who observe you, that He who in reality has no one else capable of honouring will honour you with kinds of honours, just as you showed mercy to your brothers by honouring them against the corruption of relations among them, which is the destroyer.

The verse indicates that sin other than disbelief does not expel one from faith; that reconciliation is among the greatest acts of obedience; and that it is obligatory to support the oppressed, since fighting is not permitted without it being obligatory. Al-Qushayri said: This indicates the great burden of the one who tells tales, the gossip-monger, and the one who incites discord in corrupting relations among people. He also said: Among the conditions of brotherhood is that you do not make your brother need to seek your help or ask you for support, and that you do not fall short in attending to his circumstances to the point that his need becomes unclear to you, so that he is forced to ask you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 49, verse 11:

When He forbade hastening to pass judgment upon merely hearing what would give rise to strife, and concluded with that by which mercy is hoped for, and since the report which Allah, glorified is He, commanded to be verified might well be clear, He forbade the things that cause evil, which the report conveys, so that they become a cause of rancour, from which evil arises, which is a cause of vengeance. (This is) mercy for the servants of Allah and a hope of mercy from Him. (p-375) Thus He said, as a consequence of that, mentioning what is in the fourth section of the manners and benefits, namely the obligation to abandon harming the believers in their presence, and belittling their condition, which removes their joy and brings about their harm: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, that is, those who have brought about the affirmation through assent, ﴿let not a people ridicule﴾, that is, let them not mock and humiliate.

Since mockery takes place in the presence of people, He said, expressing by what implies that whoever participates, or consents, or remains silent while being able, is a mocker who shares with the speaker: ﴿a people﴾, that is, men who have the strength of striving. In the expression by this there is a stirring toward a person standing over himself and restraining it [from what it desires] of deficiencies, in gratitude for the strength Allah has given: ﴿a people [ridiculing] a people﴾, for that necessitates evil; because the weakest of people, when stirred to belittle, grows strong by what arises in him of self-interest.

Since what sound judgment requires is that a person does not humiliate anyone except one who is secure that he will not at some time become stronger than him in this world and in the Hereafter, He gave the reason with His saying: ﴿perhaps﴾, that is, because it is fitting and likely for them that ﴿they [the ridiculed] may be better than them﴾, so the matter reverses against them and they suffer an evil end. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Affliction is entrusted to speech, and if I ridicule a dog, I fear that I would be transformed into a dog." (p-376) Al-Qushayri said: "No one belittles another except that he is subjected to it, and one should not judge by the outward conditions of people, for in the corners are hidden things, and the Truth, glorified is He, conceals His friends behind the veil of suspicion." Likewise in the report: "How many a dishevelled, dust-covered one with two worn garments, whom no one regards, would, if he swore by Allah, have Allah fulfil it for him."

Since the application of "a people" is to those who have the capacity to resist, namely men, He said, expressing what applies to women with the vowel of nun opened, that abandoning action (is required): ﴿nor women [ridiculing] women﴾. Then He gave the reason for the prohibition with His saying: ﴿perhaps﴾, that is, they should fear lest ﴿they [the ridiculed] may be better than them﴾, that is, the mockers.

Since mockery includes disparagement and is not stated openly in it, and since defamation is disparagement itself, He raised the matter to it, saying: ﴿And do not defame﴾, that is, do not find fault in a hidden manner, ﴿yourselves﴾, by one of you finding fault with another by a gesture or the like, how much more so when it is done openly; for you, in mutual connection and compassion, are like a single soul. Or a person does what is blamed, so he has defamed himself, or defames another, so his defaming of him becomes a cause for the other to search for his faults and defame him, so that he is the one who defamed himself. ﴿And do not insult one another with nicknames﴾, that is, let one of you not call another by a name, that is, calling out in a manner of altering and debasing, ﴿by nicknames﴾, by one calling his companion with a title that displeases him, whether he was the one who first coined it. As for nicknames of praise, how excellent they are, like al-Siddiq and al-Faruq. (p-377)

Since faith is a restraint upon persistent disobedience, and since insulting and mockery sever that restraint, He gave the reason with what indicates that it is wickedness, expressing with the word that comprises all blameworthy qualities, as a warning against it, saying: ﴿Wretched is the name of wickedness﴾, that is, departing from the bond of religion ﴿after faith﴾. He omitted the preposition, as a notice that whoever falls into this is about to be constantly attached to it, so that it engrosses his time; for the soul is fond of deficiencies, especially those in which there is exaltation. So whoever does that has consented for himself to be branded with wickedness after having been described as a believer.

Since the implied sense is: "Whoever repents, those are the rightly guided," and since the context calls for warning more fittingly, He conjoined to it His saying: ﴿And whoever does not repent﴾, that is, does not return from what Allah has forbidden, thereby lightening upon himself what had been made heavy upon him, ﴿those﴾, that is, the far removed from Allah, ﴿they are﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the extreme ones in placing things other than in their proper places.

Since a person may sometimes call his companion by a nickname, not intending to disparage him, or do an action that resembles mockery, without intending mockery, the Exalted forbade hastening to suspicion without verification (*tathabbut*), because that is placing things in other than their proper places, which is the meaning of injustice (*zulm*). He concluded with the fifth oath, alerting to what it contains of (p-٣٧٨) lofty and precious meanings: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, meaning those who acknowledged faith, even if they are at its first stage. ﴿Avoid﴾, meaning: obligate yourselves to abandon and keep away, and place at a far side from you ﴿much of suspicion﴾, meaning regarding people and others. So be cautious with every suspicion, and do not persist with it until you are certain of it, lest you proceed on its basis to the evil it requires, except after clarifying its truth from its falsehood, by a sound sign appearing to you and a clear cause. Investigating that which gave rise to the suspicion is not forbidden, just as the Prophet ﷺ investigated in the incident of the slander (*ifk*) and verified until the certain news came to him from God. This implies that much of it is to be avoided, as in *ijtihad* where there is no decisive proof, and as in thinking well of God, the Exalted; rather, it may be obligatory, as the Exalted said: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believing men and believing women not think well of their own kind?﴾ [al-Nur: 12]. The indefinite form (*tankir*) conveys the generality of the prohibition over every suspicion, so it carries the sense of "some" (*ba'd*), with the assurance that much of it is forbidden to undertake except after clarifying its matter. Had it been known, it would imply that it is avoided only when it is abundant. Al-Qushayri said: "The self does not affirm, the heart does not deny, and distinguishing between self and heart is difficult. Whoever still retains any portion of his own shares, however small, has no right to claim the clarity of the heart; rather, as long as some remnant of it remains in him, he is the self itself. He must suspect his own self in everything that occurs to him of the deficiency of others." (p-٣٧٩) Then he explained that by pointing out that the intelligent person is one who restrains himself from even the slightest possibility of harm, with emphatic caution, because people's actions under suspicion are the actions of one who is certain that he is free of sin. ﴿Indeed, some suspicion is sin﴾, meaning: a wrong that brings its doer to deserve punishment, like suspicion regarding the foundations of the religion, and where a decisive proof contradicts it. Al-Zamakhshari, may God have mercy on him, said: "The hamza in *ithm* (sin) is from the *waw*, as if it (suspicion) breaks the deeds, meaning it shatters them by nullifying them."

When He forbade following suspicion, He followed it with what branches from it, saying: ﴿And do not spy﴾, meaning: do not delve deeply into searching for faults, and this occurs only regarding those who conceal themselves.

Since backbiting (*ghiba*) is more general than spying, He said: ﴿And let not some of you backbite others﴾, meaning: let him not deliberately mention, in his absence, ﴿some of you about others﴾ with what he would dislike. Al-Qushayri said: "Backbiting among creatures arises only from heedlessness of the Truth." Abu Hayyan said: Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "Backbiting is the relish of the dogs of people."

Since tearing apart people's honor is like tearing apart their hide, and that is not possible for the one by whose grandeur subsistence is maintained, just as his honor is a covering over him; and because he cannot defend himself on account of his absence, like his death; and the actions of the mouth and the belly in all of that, (p-٣٨٠) and if the intelligent person reflected on this, he would find it to be of utmost repugnance; but because it is hidden, it does not occur to his mind. He made it manifest to him in His saying, affirming and expressing by "love" what is in utmost abhorrence, because of what the backbiter finds in it of desire [in backbiting], so that the depiction by this would repel him from it and make him hate it: ﴿Would any of you love﴾. He generalized with His saying ﴿any of you﴾, and expressed with *an* and the verb as a depiction of the act, saying ﴿to eat﴾, and increased the repugnance by placing it in a human being who is a brother, saying ﴿the flesh of his brother﴾, and He concluded the matter with His saying ﴿dead﴾.

Since the answer is definitively "no one would love that," He pointed to it by what caused it, with His saying ﴿so you would hate it﴾, meaning: by reason of what was mentioned, naturally. So how much more fitting it is that you hate backbiting, which is forbidden by reason, because the caller of reason is perceptive and knowing, while the caller of nature is blind and ignorant. The Glorified has arranged these wisdoms in the most wondrous order: He commanded verification (*tathabbut*). And since it may leave behind resentment, He forbade acting on its requirement of mockery, deriding, insulting by nicknames, and persisting with it, along with what such things spread of suspicions. If the self refuses except to persist with suspicion, it must not reach spying and searching for faults. If one comes upon such faults, he should refrain from mentioning them, strive to conceal them, and do all of that out of fear of God alone, nothing else. If he falls into any of that, he should hasten to repentance, hoping for reward.

(p-٣٨١) Since the implied meaning was: "So leave it, because of their hatred of what I have depicted," He linked to it what indicates the greatest cause, which is the fear of God, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And fear God﴾, meaning: make between yourselves and the Greatest King a shield by abandoning that, and by reconciling what lies between you.

Since the implied meaning was: "Indeed God accepts your repentance if you abandon it," He gave the reason with what indicates that this is an attribute of His with repeated effect, saying: ﴿Indeed God﴾, meaning the Greatest King, ﴿is Oft-Returning﴾, meaning: He repeatedly accepts repentance, and repentance is returning from disobedience to the state that was before it, in how the repentant is treated, even if he repeats the sin. So let no one despair, however many and great his sins may be. ﴿Merciful﴾, adding to that that He honors him to the utmost degree of honor.

When He, glorified is He, mentioned the religious brotherhood, reminding them through the tender bond that calls for honour and prevents retaliation, and forbade matters that self-admiration leads to through glorifying one's forefathers and the nobility of a lofty lineage, He dropped that and made clear that there is no lineage except what faith produces, the faith that began with piety. He expressed this with wording that indicates wavering and instability, pointing to the lowliness of the rank of one who boasts of lineage, and to the fact that whoever does not take warning from what has passed, and rises above the rank of those who believe, has fallen into a great lowliness: ﴿O mankind﴾, that is, all of you, believer and other, ﴿Indeed We﴾, with Our majesty and power, ﴿created you﴾, that is, brought you into being from nonexistence (p. 382) in the measures in which you exist, in your forms, and in the diversity of your branching, which exceeds counting, and We brought forth each one of you ﴿from a male﴾, who is the one intended for resolve and strength, ﴿and a female﴾, who is the place of weakness and rest. None of you has any superiority over another in this, and there is no pride in lineage.

Since their being divided into groups, each of which is known by its own name, is a remarkable matter, He expressed it with the plural of majesty and said: ﴿And We made you﴾, that is, by Our majesty, ﴿peoples (shu'ub)﴾, branching out from a single origin. Shu'ub is the plural of sha'b, with a fatha, and it is the first of the six levels of lineage among the Arabs. ﴿And tribes (qaba'il)﴾ are beneath the peoples; ﴿clans ('imarah)﴾ beneath the tribes; ﴿sub-clans (butun)﴾ beneath the clans; ﴿branches (afkhadh)﴾ beneath the sub-clans; ﴿families (fasa'il)﴾ beneath the branches; and ﴿households ('ashair)﴾ beneath the families. Khuzaymah is a people (sha'b), Kinanah is a tribe (qabilah), Quraysh is a clan ('imarah), Qusayy is a sub-clan (batn), 'Abd Manaf is a branch (fakhdh), Hashim is a family (fasilah), and al-'Abbas is a household ('ashirah). Al-Baghawi said: "There is no living group after the household that can be described by it." End of quote. He limited the mention to the first two because they are the furthest levels a human can easily know, and what is below them is more appropriate. Then he mentioned the reason for the division so that it may be pondered, and said: ﴿that you may know one another﴾, that is, so that a person may know those who are close to him in lineage, in order to join the ties of kinship that are due to him, not so that you may boast and pride yourselves over one another.

Since the purpose of boasting by描述 of ancestry among them was honour toward whoever was most boastful (p. 383), the preceding verse, which this verse follows, commanded piety, so the implied meaning is: "Then fear Allah regarding your relatives and your kin." So He said, nullifying boasting by lineages, giving the reason for what the context guided us to infer, and emphasising because of what they held, namely that nobility comes only through lineage: ﴿Indeed, the most honourable of you﴾, O boasters, ﴿in the sight of Allah﴾, that is, the King to whom no one has any command, and there is no noble one except him whom He honours with His nobility, and no perfection belongs to anyone other than Him, ﴿is the most righteous (atqakum) of you﴾. That is the male whose origin is sound through following his father Adam, peace be upon him, so he does not incline toward femininity, even if he is lowest in lineage. This is why He emphasised it. This is the meaning of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The best of you in the Jahiliyyah are the best of you in Islam, when they gain understanding." That is, when they know, having the faculty of understanding (fiqh), and act upon what they know, as al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The faqih is only the one who acts upon his knowledge." It has already been mentioned that this is what is intended by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [az-Zumar: 9], by what its context and what precedes it indicate. The most pious does not boast over others, because he does not believe that he is the most pious. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': "The noblest of nobility is piety, which is the gathering of human virtues, and the basest of baseness is immorality. This is because nobility is a name for praiseworthy actions, and these actions are praiseworthy only when they are from knowledge and aimed at Allah, and this is piety. So piety is nothing but knowledge and the pursuit of praiseworthy actions." End of quote. That is because piety establishes perfections and negates deficiencies, so its possessor becomes human yet angelic (p. 384).

Since this was fixed in their natures, firmly implanted in their dispositions, and inherited among them, namely that boasting is only through lineages, and that the noble one is only the one whose origin is pure, and since uprooting this from their souls, in what Allah, glorified is He, has established as custom in the abode of causes, requires emphasis, He, glorified is He, emphasised it, giving the reason for His statement, which informs them of who is most honourable: ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, that is, the One encompassing in knowledge and power, ﴿is All-Knowing﴾, that is, of utmost knowledge of the outward, ﴿All-Aware﴾, encompassing knowledge of the inward and the secrets as well. Al-Baghawi related, with a chain through 'Abdullah ibn Humayd, from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet ﷺ circled the Ka'bah on the day of the Conquest on his mount, to touch the corners with his staff. When he went out he found no place to kneel his mount, so he descended upon the hands of men. Then he stood and addressed them, praised Allah and extolled Him, and said: "Praise be to Allah who has removed from you the arrogance of the Jahiliyyah and its pride in forefathers. People are of two kinds: a pious, righteous one who is honourable before Allah, and a wicked, miserable one who is lowly before Allah." Then he recited: ﴿O mankind﴾ — the verse. Then he said: "I say this word of mine, and I ask Allah's forgiveness for myself and for you." Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi [who graded it as hasan], and al-Bayhaqi also narrated it. Al-Mundhiri said, with a [good] chain, and the wording is his, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, has removed from you the arrogance of the Jahiliyyah and its pride in forefathers. People are the children of Adam, and Adam is from dust: a believer who is pious, and a wicked one who is miserable. Let people cease boasting over men who are only coal from the coal of Hell, or they will be more lowly before Allah than the dung beetles that push filth with their noses." (p. 385)

When Allah, glorified is He, commanded the honouring and magnifying of His Messenger (ﷺ), forbade harming him personally or harming his community, and forbade boasting, which is the cause of severing ties and mutual hostility, He concluded with the attribute of a report. He indicated this by His saying [pointing] that nothing of what He commanded or forbade is counted except with sincerity (ikhlas). So He said: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed."﴾ That is, the people of the desert, from Banu Asad and others, who are the source of harshness [and rudeness], those whose discipline was already mentioned in Surat al-Fath. He attached the ta' to their verb, indicating their weakness in resolve. Ibn Burjan said: "They are a people who bore witness to the truth while not knowing what they bore witness to, except that their souls [were not] pulling them toward denial." ﴿"We have believed."﴾ [That is], in all that you have brought, so we have complied with what we were commanded in this surah, and we have pure lineage, so we are more noble than others among the people of the settled towns (madar).

Since faith (iman) is the assent of the heart, no human can have access to it except by Allah's granting him access to it, so they were lying in their claim. He said: ﴿Say﴾, that is, as a denial of them, while observing courtesy by not explicitly calling them liars: ﴿"You have not believed."﴾ That is, your hearts have not assented. For if you had believed, you would not have counted your faith as a favour, because faith is assent to all of Allah's perfections, among which is that without His favour through guidance, faith would not have been attained. So the favour and bounty belong to Him and to His Messenger (ﷺ), through whose hands this came about.

Since the original sense of the response should have been, "So do not say, 'We have believed,' for that is a lie," and He turned away from this to avoid forbidding the claim of faith, He followed it with His saying: ﴿But say, "We have submitted."﴾ because you have submitted for the sake of the world, not for the sake of religion. He turned away from it so that it would not become a testimony in their favour of Islam in general. ﴿"We have submitted"﴾, that is, we have shown outward submission to the outward rulings, so we are safe from being a party to the believers and a helper to the polytheists. It is said: aslama al-rajul (the man submitted) when he entered into peace (silm), just as one says ashta (he entered winter) when he entered the winter. He did not say, "But you have submitted," because that would contain testimony in their favour of Islam necessarily accompanied by the faith that is being negated, so it would be a contradiction. The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two contrasting elements are mentioned, each one's counterpart being implied by the other): the negation of legal faith first indicates the affirmation of linguistic submission second, and the command to say "we have submitted" second indicates the prohibition of saying "we have believed" first.

Since "lamma" (not yet) is not exhaustive, He followed it with what covers all the time that has passed, so that the ruling of their not having believed would be framed by the command to limit themselves to reporting their submission. So He said, informing that what they strive to conceal is exposed to Him: ﴿Does He not know who created?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14] ﴿And faith has not yet entered﴾ [that is], up to this time ﴿into your hearts﴾, [that is], complete knowledge. So the utterance of the tongue is not counted as faith unless the heart is in agreement with it. ﴿So you disobeyed Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) and nullified your deeds.﴾ The expression "lamma" implies that they believed after that. It is possible that what is meant by this negation is the negation of firm establishment in the heart, not the negation of entry altogether, as evidenced by: ﴿The believers are only those...﴾ [al-Hujurat: 15], rather than "Those who believed are only..."

Since the implied sense is: "If you believe, Allah will know that from your hearts, independent of your saying," He followed it with, encouraging them to repent: ﴿And if you obey Allah﴾, that is, the King whose opponent does not feel secure from His punishment, ﴿and His Messenger﴾, whose obedience is from the obedience to Him, in accordance with the outward state you are in, so that your hearts will believe, ﴿He will not deprive you﴾, that is, He will not diminish or cheat you, from lātahu yalītuhu, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. The two Basran readers recited yā'lit-kum from al-alt, which is also diminution, and this is the dialect of Asad and Ghatafan. These two are the ones addressed by this verse and rebuked by it. Abu Hayyan said: Mujahid said: "It was revealed concerning [Banu] Asad ibn Khuzayma." End of quotation. For this reason Abu 'Amr chose this recitation and turned away from the dialect of the Hijaz.

﴿Of your deeds, anything﴾, so there is no need to inform Him of your faith by other than what indicates it of statements and actions. Ibn Burjan said: "The common people and most of the heedless are Muslims but not believers. If they know with knowledge what they bore witness to and fixed upon, a knowledge with certainty, then they are the believers." In the verse there is ihtibak from another aspect: He mentioned the absence of faith first as an indication of its affirmation second, and He mentioned the complete preservation of deeds second as an indication of their diminution or nullification first. Its secret is that He negated the foundation of good first and encouraged obedience second by preserving what they had toiled over of deeds.

Since man is built upon deficiency, if he were left to his own deeds he would perish, and his deeds would be lost through the deficiency that befalls them. He said, appealing to them [to] repentance, emphasising it as an alert that it is something that deserves emphasis, [because creatures] do not do the like of it: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿is Forgiving﴾, that is, Veiling of lapses and faults for whoever repents and whose intention is sound, and for others when He wills, so there is no reproach and no punishment. ﴿Merciful﴾, that is, He adds to the veiling the great honour of generosity.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 49, verse 15:

When He negated faith from them, and a person might sometimes err regarding himself [and think] that he is a believer when he is not so, He informed of the believer by way of restriction (ḥaṣr), mentioning its outward and inward sign, which are the mothers of virtues (ummahāt al-faḍā'il): knowledge ('ilm), chastity ('iffa) and courage (shajā'a). So He said, in answer to one who says, "Who then has believed?", turning away from a direct answer to a description of the firmly rooted (al-rāsikh), as an encouragement to take on his description, and as a notice that one who informs about himself of the sign of his faith intends only that he is firmly rooted: ﴿Indeed the believers﴾, that is, those deeply established (al-'arīqūn) in faith, which is the life of hearts. Al-Qushayrī said: Hearts do not live except after the slaughter of souls, (p-389) and souls do not die but they do live. ﴿Those who have believed﴾, that is, those who affirmed, acknowledging ﴿in God﴾, holding to all that He has of attributes of perfection, ﴿and His Messenger﴾, bearing witness to his message. This is the recognition (ma'rifa) which is knowledge ('ilm), and whose end is wisdom (ḥikma). This affirmation here indicates that what is negated, according to what has been said, is perfection and not the absolute, for otherwise He would have said, "Indeed those who have believed."

And since this is great, and steadfastness in it is greater, and it is the very essence of wisdom, He pointed to the great excellence of steadfastness by His saying: ﴿Then﴾, that is, after mounting this great rank, ﴿they did not doubt﴾, that is, they did not contend with the original nature (al-fiṭra al-ūlā) by deliberately causing doubt, and they did not allow doubt to occur at any time after faith. Thus, through the lengthening of times and the occurrence of trials, their description remains fresh and new after doubt. Perhaps He expressed it in the form of al-iftiʿāl (ilti'āl, "they did not doubt") as an indication of pardon for the inward talk of the self (ḥadīth al-nafs), whose origin a person cannot repel, and which he hates to the utmost degree and strives to repel. So, when he gives it breath, walks along with it and prolongs it, that is the blameworthy thing, until it becomes firmly established.

And since He mentioned the inward sign in a manner comprising all the financial and bodily acts of worship, He said: ﴿And they strove﴾, that is, they carried out striving (jihād) with everything in which the self ought to exert itself, confirming what they had claimed with their tongues of faith, ﴿with their wealth﴾, and that is chastity ('iffa), ﴿and their selves﴾, which is more general than intention and other things, and that is courage (shajā'a). He mentioned wealth first because it was scarce among the Arabs at that time. ﴿In the way of God﴾, that is, the path of the Supreme King, by fighting the disbelievers and other acts of worship that require wealth and self, not those who hold back and say: "Our wealth and our families have occupied us." Al-Qushayrī said: God made faith conditional upon the qualities He mentioned, and He mentioned it with the word "innamā" (indeed/only), which is for affirmation and implies both inclusion and exclusion. So whoever separates faith from its conditions which He has set for it, his claim is rejected, and faith is security for the servant; a faith that does not bring security to its possessor, its opposite is more fitting for him.

And since He identified them by mentioning their sign by way of restriction, that produced another restriction, cutting off the hopes of the claimants, in a manner by which He praised them with what is greatly esteemed by them, encouraging the like of their state. So He said: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the high-ranking ones, for whom there was attained the balance of character and justice in religion with all the mothers of good character, ﴿they are﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿the truthful﴾, in speech, state and deed. As for others, they are liars.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 49, verse 16:

Since they were, as it were, saying: "We are such," he (ﷺ) was commanded to rebuke them and reproach them, as a sign of what the conclusion of the verse indicated, namely the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, by which the truthful is distinguished from others among all creation. So He said: (p-391) ﴿Say﴾, that is, to these Bedouins, addressing them in a manner that makes them appear ignorant and rebuking them: ﴿Will you inform Allah of your religion?﴾, that is, will you inform Him with a great and eloquent information? It is as if, when they believed, that was an informing from them, and when they said "We have believed," that was a repetition, so it took the form of teaching, and He rebuked them for that: ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, encompassing in power and knowledge, ﴿[knows] your religion﴾, and therefore you say: "We have believed." In this there is a kind of good news for them, because He brought religion into existence for them and attributed it to them. Ibn Burjan said this.

When He had denied them and rebuked them, He joined to it what bears witness to it, so He said: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, while the King encompassing all things ﴿knows what is in the heavens﴾, all of them, despite their greatness and the abundance of what is in them and who is in them. Since the context was one of refutation and rebuke of them, it was the place for emphasis, so He said: ﴿and what is on the earth﴾, likewise.

Since the context called for generality, He stated the name explicitly rather than using a pronoun, lest it be taken to restrict the matter to the creatures mentioned, so He said: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One to whom belongs complete encompassing ﴿of every thing﴾, that is, of what has been mentioned and what has not been mentioned, ﴿is Knowing﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 49, verse 17:

Since their statement takes the form of a favour (*al-minna*), He said, rebuking them for it and addressing them in the present tense to depict the ugliness of their state: ﴿They count it a favour upon you﴾. That is, they mention it as one who has done a good deed (*sana'a*) for you and conferred a blessing upon you, as if they did it only because you needed it, not seeking reward for it. This is because *al-mann* (conferring a favour and reminding of it) is *al-qat'* (cutting off, severing). In the *Kashshaf* he said: "Because one who bestows it upon another does so only to cut off his need with it, and not with any intention of seeking a reward, and then it is said: 'So-and-so has a claim upon him' (*ḍay'a*), when he regards it as a favour and a kindness upon him." Since Islam is apparent in religion, which is submission outwardly together with the acceptance of the inner heart, He did not express it with that word, but said: ﴿And if they embrace Islam﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 20], that is, they have actually submitted outwardly to the rulings.

Since *al-mann* is the cutting off of a gift upon which no recompense is expected, He said: ﴿Say﴾, that is, in reply to their statement: ﴿Do not count it a favour upon me﴾. He expressed it with the word *al-mann* to indicate that Islam's reward is sought only from God, so it is not right to regard it as a good deed done to anyone, for that corrupts it. ﴿Your Islam upon me﴾, supposing you were Muslims, that is, adherents of the religion of Islam, which is outward submission together with inner acceptance. [That is], do not mention it as a favour at all. The verb ﴿do not count it a favour﴾ (*tamunnū*) is here implicitly containing the meaning "mention" (*tadhkurū*) itself, not merely its sense, as was explained in ﴿and that you may glorify God for having guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

﴿But God﴾, that is, the Supreme King, to whom belongs the favour over every existing thing and who is under no obligation of favour to anyone in any way, ﴿confers a favour upon you﴾, that is, He mentions that He has bestowed upon you His blessings, both outward and inward, among them ﴿that﴾, that is, in that ﴿He guided you to faith﴾, that is, He made it clear to you or enabled you to be guided, which is the affirmation of the heart together with outward submission. Expressing this as a favour is most fitting, for He, glory be to Him, has no need of any deed, since no benefit reaches Him and no harm. He sought deeds only for the benefit of the doers themselves. He conferred a favour upon them by sending His Messenger ﷺ, who made clear to them, yet they all denied him.
